issue_context.title: LHASH statistical counter performance overheads (cache contention)
issue_context.body:
Currently LHASH has a number of statistical counters like `num_hash_calls`, `num_comp_calls`, `num_retrieve`, `num_retrieve_miss` and `num_hash_comps`. These are incremented using atomics during retrieval operations, which creates possible cache contention issues with high amounts of parallelism. This causes `getrn` to sometimes be more costly than it needs to be.

This seems needless since these statistics are probably very rarely used in production. They are only used by various OPENSSL_LH_ statistical functions which output text reports to BIOs.

Possibly we should simply compile these out when `OPENSSL_NO_TRACE` is defined (or another define if someone has a better suggestion).

It is a valid question whether the other LHASH counters should also be compiled out in this case. Since these other counters are only touched on mutating LHASH operations, they do not use atomics because the caller of LHASH mutation operations has responsibility for synchronization. But for consistency and performance we may as well compile these out at the same time.

It is possible this is a cause of #16791 (MSQUIC handshakes per second performance regression) but this is mostly speculative on my part, and based on extrapolating profiling run on my machine to how that profiling might perform when extrapolated to a very high-core-count server.

review_comments:
We still need the `lh->error = 0;` side effect of this.

This was left using tsan because I'm paranoid :)

Having this mutation on read-only access to the LHASH isn't ideal, but I guess it'll probably be put in a write buffer by high performance hardware, and we need it to meet API. As an aside, anyone know if modern hardware does an equality comparison before changing a shared cache line from shared to modified (MESI)?
